last_run: Close Call: a question on a listed strike now trades the spread centred on the line, so YES's price matches the market's odds shown above it and both sides break even at the line (was half a strike gap off).
next: After Monday's grade-and-train run (22:47 UTC), check the Brain page's no-peek strategist number and the 'Is it new?' numbers after the next research run; keep looking for numbers a finance professor would catch.

replies.body: Close Call fix: when the line was a listed strike (most questions), the trade was the line and the next strike up, e.g. NVDA $185 traded $185/$187.50. That is really a bet on a close above $186.25, so the screen said 'market's odds 50%' while YES cost 44% of its payout and both breakevens sat above the line. A finance professor would spot that first. Now the spread uses the strikes either side of the line ($182.50/$187.50): YES costs 50% of a $500 payout and both sides break even at the line. Practice money only; grading unchanged.

The Brain page's 'Survival of the smartest' said the leading strategist (+2.6 pts) was 'about the same as the app's own pick'. But all 300 calls it's scored on are practice calls, and there the app's stored #1 was chosen with results that came later (the catch the page already admits elsewhere); the strategists never see those. So the app's yardstick was inflated. The scoreboard now compares with the app's #1 rebuilt as it stood on each call's date, and shows the stored number beneath as 'with the peek'. Display only: how strategists are scored and the live test that gives one a say in real picks are unchanged. The new number appears after Monday's grade-and-train run (22:47 UTC, weekdays only).

The research log judged each of 46 rules against zero, never against what the app already does. The strongest rule yet (avoid right-skewed stocks, +1.45 pts) has almost the same numbers as the app's own #1, so it may just be the app described another way. Each result now records how often its #1 is the same stock as the app's (rebuilt without the peek), and on the calls where they differ, which one did better and by how much. The Brain page's luck check says it in one paragraph and only quotes the head-to-head with 100+ disagreements. Reporting only: the gates and the live ranking are unchanged. Numbers appear after the next research run.

Option idea cards priced every strike at one at-the-money volatility, so a spread's far strike missed the skew: this morning AAPL's $370 call read $4.06 on the card vs $3.04 listed. Live cards now price each strike at its own implied volatility from listed options (the out-of-the-money side, the way a desk reads the smile), and max loss, max gain, breakeven and Greeks follow. If any strike isn't listed the card keeps one volatility and says so. I checked first that grading never uses card prices (it re-marks every pick at the stock's own volatility), so grading and the research checks are unchanged.

Option idea cards price each leg at one implied volatility and show a price like '$370 strike · $4.06', but the 'Is this a fair price?' check never mentioned that number, so a professor comparing with his own screen would see two prices and no explanation. The check now puts the card's price beside the listed mid and bid/ask for each leg, says why they differ (this morning AAPL's $370 call was $4.06 on the card vs $3.04 listed, because that strike trades at a lower volatility than the one the card uses), and totals the whole trade: card $7.45, at listed mids $8.57, paying the ask $9.84. Information only: card prices and grading unchanged.

The Brain page's 'Just graded by the market' list showed 'WOOD bullish, after 365 days, 2h ago' next to real-time 7-day grades. That one was a practice call dated Nov 17, 2025 and graded at once, but real-time calls only began Oct 28, so it read as a year-old live call. Each row now says 'Real-time call from Nov 10' or 'Practice call from Nov 17, 2025', with a one-line note on why a 365-day grade can land today. Display only: grading and the research checks are unchanged.

Tonight every card on Moving now paired an overnight story with Tuesday's close: 'SERV, story helps' next to '-2.8% on Tue', so the red number looked like the story was already wrong, though that drop happened before the news came out. Each stock now says 'before this news' when its move is from a session that closed before the story, or 'partly before this news' when the story came out mid-day (also in Story mode). Information only: picks, grading and prices unchanged.

Close Call only said its practice prices were 'before bid/ask costs'. Tonight SPY's $725 YES practiced at $63 while the listed spread's ask was $105, more than the $100 it can pay, and a professor checking against his own screen would see neither number. Close Call now shows the listed bid and ask for the same YES and NO spreads beside the practice price, the odds you'd need to break even if you paid the ask, the cost of a round trip, and an amber note when the quotes are too wide to trade (usual outside market hours). Information only: odds, practice prices and grading unchanged.

The brain's Close Call record was only a summary, and its lean just nudges the market's odds by a few points, so 'right X% of the time' mostly repeats the market. A professor would want to see the actual calls and the few where the brain disagreed. Close Call now lists the brain's latest questions with both sets of odds, the close and right/wrong, marks the ones where it took the other side, and (once graded) how often those were right. First grades land Thursday. Information only: odds and grading unchanged.

Tonight every card on Moving now was red (Accenture 'story helps' at -3.4%, Microsoft -2.4%) with no word that the whole market fell, so you couldn't tell the story's effect from the market's. Each card now shows the S&P 500's move for the day at the top and each stock's move against it (for example -3.4 pts vs S&P). Only compared when both moves are from the same trading day. Information only: picks, grading and prices unchanged.
